setting: a dental practice management software vendor (Brightsmile Systems)
prompt: I’m the product lead at Brightsmile Systems and need a quick but thorough take for our CFO, Maya Patel. We’re planning to raise the monthly subscription for our flagship practice‑management suite from $99 to $119 effective 1 Oct 2024 (our Q3 rollout). We currently have 5,200 active practices, a churn rate that has hovered around 4 % per month, and we spend roughly $1,200 to acquire each new customer. Our internal model says the average practice stays with us 36 months, giving an LTV of $4,320 (we’ve just added the $5 per‑user support surcharge into the cost side). I’m assuming the price hike won’t push churn beyond the existing 4 % baseline, and that the $20 increase will lift ARR by $12.5 M by year‑end 2025. What I don’t know is whether our main competitor, ClearDental, will launch a discount program in Q4 that could undercut us by $10. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, the main ways this could fail (e.g., churn spike, hidden support costs, competitor reaction), and the result that would make us stop or pivot—specifically if churn climbs above 6 % in the first two months after the price change.

setting: a university alumni-donations office (Kestrel University Advancement)
prompt: I’m the senior manager for the Kestrel University Advancement office and need a quick but solid briefing for Dr. Maya Patel, our Vice President of Advancement, about the proposed “Impact Circle” tiered giving program we plan to launch on 15 Oct 2024. The idea is to shift our current flat $2,500 annual donor ask to a three‑tier structure: $1,500, $2,500, and $5,000. We estimate we can enroll 200 donors in the first year, with 30 % of them moving to the $5,000 tier, yielding an expected revenue of $500,000 (200 × $2,500) plus an extra $150,000 from the upgrades (60 × $2,500). I’m assuming the upgrade conversion will happen within six months and that our acquisition cost remains $12,000 per donor. We haven’t factored in the 2.5 % payment‑processing fee or a potential 10 % attrition rate after the first year—both are unknowns. Please give Dr. Patel one clear recommendation (go ahead, modify, or pause), list the three biggest ways this could fail, and tell us what result—e.g., net revenue falling below $450,000 after costs—would make us stop or re‑evaluate the program. Thanks.

setting: a meal-kit company for athletes (Ironplate Meals)
prompt: I'm drafting a proposal for our COO, Maya Patel, to raise the price of the Ironplate Pro kit from $65 to $77 starting 2024-06-01. We currently have 30,000 active subscribers, each paying $65 monthly, generating $1.95M in revenue. Variable cost per kit is $30 and shipping averages $15, so gross profit per kit is $20. Our CAC is $45 and churn has been 5% per month, which we assume will stay constant. We estimate LTV at $360 (12 months × $30 net profit). The board wants a single recommendation, the main ways this could fail, and the trigger that would make us stop or pivot. I calculated that the $12 price lift would add $360,000 in monthly profit (30,000 × $12), but I may have missed the fact that a 10% price elasticity could cause a 15% drop in subscribers, cutting revenue by $292,500. We also don’t know the new regulatory fee for enhanced protein labeling, which could be $0.50 per kit. Please include the numbers, point out any arithmetic or missing cost issues, and give the recommendation for Maya.

setting: a legal-document automation startup for solo lawyers (Clause & Co)
prompt: I need a quick briefing for our CFO, Maya Patel, about whether we should roll out the new “SmartClause” subscription tier next quarter. The tier would be $49 per month for solo practitioners, down from our current $79, and we’d bundle the existing document library plus a premium AI‑drafting add‑on. We project 1,200 sign‑ups by the end of Q3 2024 based on a 6 % conversion from the 20,000 free‑trial users we have now, assuming a 30‑day trial period. Our current ARR is $120,000, churn is 5 % monthly, and we have a runway of 12 months with $2.1 M in cash. We’re counting on a 10 % increase in cross‑sell revenue from existing customers, which we calculated as $120,000 × 1.10 = $132,000, but I suspect we may have double‑counted the expansion. The only unknown is the compliance cost of handling data for the new California privacy law, which we haven’t priced yet. Please give me one clear recommendation for Maya, list the main ways this pricing change could fail, and tell me what metric or event would make us stop or pivot the rollout. Thanks.

setting: a hospital outpatient scheduling team (St. Mara Outpatient)
prompt: I’m the scheduling lead for St. Mara Outpatient and I need a quick briefing for our CFO, Laura Greene, on whether we should launch the new digital check‑in platform we’re piloting. Our current average appointment revenue is $150 and the direct cost per visit is $70, which we (mistakenly) calculated as an 85 % gross margin, but the correct margin is actually $80 (≈53 %). The no‑show rate sits at 12 % and we expect the platform’s automated reminders to cut that to 8 %; each reminder costs $0.10 and the service fees are $2,000 per month. We also anticipate a 15 % increase in daily throughput and a reduction of 5 full‑time admin staff at $55,000 each per year. Our annual scheduling budget is $250,000. The assumption we’re making is that the 15 % throughput boost translates line‑for‑line into revenue, ignoring any potential bottlenecks in physician availability. The unknown is the patient acceptance rate of digital check‑in, which we estimate at 70 % but have no data yet. Please give Laura one recommendation, list the main ways this rollout could fail, and tell me what specific result (e.g., less than a 3 % drop in no‑shows after three months, or total monthly costs exceeding $6,000) would make us stop or re‑evaluate the project.

setting: a fleet-electrification consultancy (Voltway Advisors)
prompt: I need a quick brief for our CFO, Maya Patel, on whether we should roll out the new “VoltFlex” lease‑to‑own package to the regional delivery fleet of QuickShip Logistics. The plan is to price the lease at $1,200 per vehicle per month, with a 24‑month term, which we estimate will generate $28.8 M in revenue (12 months × 2,000 vehicles × $1,200). We expect the hardware cost per electric van to be $45,000, the battery lease to be $5,000 per year, and installation and training to be $2,500 per unit. Our assumption is that the federal clean‑vehicle tax credit will be 30 % of the hardware cost and will apply uniformly across the fleet. We have a $3 M budget for upfront inventory, and we think we can finance the rest with a revolving line at 6 % APR. The unknown is the actual take‑up rate among QuickShip drivers after the pilot ends in September 2025. Please give Maya one clear recommendation, list the three biggest ways this rollout could fail, and tell me what metric (e.g., net cash burn exceeding $7 M after six months) would make us stop or renegotiate the deal. Note: our current breakeven calculation uses 150 vehicles × $12,000 = $1.8 M, but we may have missed the installation cost in that figure.

setting: an HR analytics platform sold to mid-size manufacturers (Peoplegrid)
prompt: Maya, I need a quick but solid recommendation for the CFO meeting next week (June 12). Peoplegrid currently bills $12 per active user per month to 250 mid‑size manufacturers, averaging 40 users each, giving us $3.2 M ARR. Our monthly churn is 6% and CAC averages $2,500 per new client. My assumption is that the price elasticity will be –0.3, so churn will stay flat. The unknown is how many customers will drop out or reduce seats because of the higher price; we have no data on price‑sensitivity for this segment. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, outline the main ways this could fail (e.g., higher churn, support cost overruns, competitive response), and tell me what metric or outcome (e.g., churn rising above 8% in the first two quarters) would make us stop or pivot the plan. The answer is for Maya Patel, our Chief Product Officer.

setting: a podcast hosting and ad-marketplace company (Echolane)
prompt: Maya Patel, our CEO, wants a clear go‑no‑go on the premium tier and the new ad‑marketplace commission change. We haven’t factored in the extra bandwidth and content‑delivery costs that the higher ad volume will incur, and we still don’t know the regulatory status of the new geo‑targeting feature we plan to launch in Q4 2025. Please give Maya one recommendation, list the main ways this plan could fail, and tell me the specific result (e.g., cash‑runway below three months or regulatory block) that would make us stop or pivot.

setting: a veterinary clinic chain (Pawprint Vets)
prompt: I’m the regional operations lead for Pawprint Vets and need a quick briefing for our CEO, Dr. Maya Patel, on whether to roll out a new preventive‑care subscription across our 12 clinics. We’ve modeled a $45 monthly fee (up from $30) that would cover two wellness exams, one vaccine, and a dental cleaning per year. Our current average revenue per pet visit is $85, with a variable cost of $45, so each visit contributes $40 to profit. We assume a 20% conversion of our 15,000 active clients within the first six months (by 31 Oct 2024) and that the subscription will reduce per‑visit cost by 10% through bulk purchasing of vaccines. Please show the numbers you use.

setting: an online used-furniture marketplace (Second Seat)
prompt: I need a quick, data‑driven opinion for Maya Patel, our CEO, on whether we should raise the seller listing fee on Second Seat from $15 to $20 starting 1 Nov 2024. Right now we have 45,000 monthly active users (MAU) and about 35 % of them list items, with an average of 1.2 listings per seller. Please give me one clear recommendation, outline the primary ways this could fail, and tell me what metric (e.g., churn >8 % or profit per listing dropping below $5) would make us stop or rethink the change.

setting: a construction-bid estimating tool (Cornerstone Bids)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal for Cornerstone Bids and need a concrete recommendation for Maya Patel, our CEO, plus the top three ways this could fail and the trigger that would make us abort. Right now we have 1,520 active subscriber firms paying $199 per month, giving us $3.6 M ARR. I’m assuming the higher price will lift our average revenue per user (ARPU) by 8 % and will increase churn from 5 % to 7 % because some smaller contractors may drop out. Our CAC has been $115 per firm, and I’m assuming it stays constant. The development cost for the new tier features is $210,000, spread over 12 months, and I’ve added a $30,000 buffer for marketing. The unknown is how long regulatory approval for the new data‑privacy module will take; estimates range from 30 to 90 days. setting: a wine-subscription direct-to-consumer brand (Vinelet)
prompt: Maya Patel, our CEO, wants me to decide whether to roll out a premium “Reserve” tier for Vinelet on March 1 2025. We currently have 12,300 active subscribers paying $120 per month, with an average cost of goods sold of $45 per kit and a gross margin of 62.5%. setting: a city transit agency's rider-information app team (Metro Line Digital)
prompt:
I’m writing to you on behalf of Maya Patel, our Chief Operations Officer, who needs a quick decision memo for the upcoming board meeting on November 12, 2024. Our rider‑information app, MetroLine Pulse, currently has 118,000 monthly active users (MAU) as of the end of Q3 2024, with a 15% month‑over‑month growth rate that we’ve been projecting linearly through Q4. Right now 31% of those users are subscribed to the premium push‑notification service at $1.99 per month, generating $7,360 in monthly subscription revenue. Advertising brings in $0.45 per user per month, or about $53,100 total. We estimate variable costs at $0.03 per user for data storage plus a fixed $5,000 for server scaling each month. 

We’re considering raising the premium price to $2.49, assuming churn will stay at 4% per month and that we can increase opt‑in to 38% by the end of the year. The unknown is the exact compliance fee we’ll incur if we expand data sharing to out‑of‑state partners (the regulator gave us a range of $8k–$12k per quarter). Please give Maya one clear recommendation on the price change, list the main ways this could fail (including any arithmetic or cost oversights you spot), and tell me what single metric—once it hits a threshold—would make us stop or pivot the plan.

setting: a developer-tools company selling a CI accelerator (Quickbuild)
prompt: Hi AI, I’m the VP of Growth at Acme DevTools and I need a concise brief for our CEO, Maya Patel, on whether we should roll out a price increase for Quickbuild next month. We currently have 12,500 paying seats at $120 per month, giving us $18 M in annual recurring revenue (ARR). I’m proposing to raise the price to $150 per seat starting 1 Nov 2024, assuming 80 % of the current users will stay and the remaining 20 % will churn at the same 4 % monthly rate we’ve seen this year. Our customer acquisition cost (CAC) is $800 per seat and the gross margin on the subscription is 70 %. I’ve calculated an LTV of $4,800 using the formula (ARPU × gross margin) ÷ churn, but I haven’t factored the extra support cost of $30 per seat per month that will rise with the higher price tier. Also, a new cloud‑provider pricing update is scheduled for 15 Oct 2024, and the exact cost impact is still unknown. Please give me one recommendation (keep or postpone the price hike), outline the main ways this could fail, and tell me what result—e.g., a month‑over‑month ARR decline of more than 5 %—would make us stop or change course.

setting: a K-12 school-district software vendor (Maple Learning Systems)
prompt: Hi, I need your help preparing a brief for Maya Patel, our CEO, about whether we should raise the subscription price for our Maple Learning platform in the upcoming fiscal year. Right now we charge $12 per student per month and serve 150,000 students across three districts, which we’ve been quoting as about $18 million in annual revenue (I’m using the $12 × 150,000 figure). The cost to deliver the service is $5 per student per month, and our current gross margin is roughly 58 %. We have a contract renewal with District 7 on March 15 2025 and we’re projecting a 12 % increase in enrollment by June 30 2025, which would add another 18,000 seats. Please give me one recommendation for Maya, outline the main ways this price change could fail, and tell me what result (e.g., churn over 4 % or a certification cost >$250k) would make us stop or reconsider.

setting: an insurance broker adding a self-serve quote tool (Anchor Mutual Brokers)
prompt: I’m the head of product at Anchor Mutual Brokers and need a quick briefing for our COO, Maya Patel, on whether we should roll out the new self‑serve quote tool on a subscription model. We have 3,500 monthly active users on the demo portal as of 15 Oct 2024, and we currently spend $9,000 per month on paid search that drives about 70 leads. Our current CAC is $120 and the average LTV of a converted policy is $1,080, assuming the average policy value stays at $1,200. setting: a boutique fitness studio chain (Tempo Studios)
prompt: I’m the head of growth at Tempo Studios and need a quick brief for our CEO, Maya Patel, on whether we should roll out a new membership price on 2025-06-01. Right now the basic monthly fee is $120, and we’re considering raising it to $140. Our latest numbers (as of March 31, 2025) show 3,200 active members, an average churn of 8% per month, and a CAC of $150 per new member. We estimate LTV at $600 based on a 12‑month average stay (120 × 12). Fixed operating costs are $210,000 per month and variable cost per member is $30. We plan to acquire 500 new members each month through a $30k marketing push, assuming the price increase won’t affect acquisition speed. The unknown is how competitors will react—whether they’ll launch a discount promotion in July. Please give Maya one recommendation (go ahead, pause, or modify), list the three main ways this plan could fail, and tell me what metric (e.g., churn exceeding 12% within two months) would make us stop or change course. Assume our runway is nine months if we stay at current burn.

setting: a nonprofit food bank scaling a donor program (Greater Valley Food Bank)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal for the new “Harvest Partners” corporate donor program at Greater Valley Food Bank and need a quick briefing for our Director of Operations, Maya Patel. Our current annual budget is $150,000, and we’ve projected we’ll need $250,000 to run the program for the next 12 months, assuming overhead stays flat at 5% of total spend. We expect to sign three anchor donors—one in March 2025, one in June 2025, and one in September 2025—each contributing $60,000, and we’re targeting a 30% retention rate for these companies year‑over‑year. The real unknown is the average corporate donor lifespan, which will affect our long‑term LTV. Please give me one recommendation on whether to launch the program now, outline the main ways it could fail (e.g., fee creep, staffing overload, donor churn), and tell me what specific result—such as a 15% higher than expected churn in the first quarter—would make us stop or change course.

setting: a regional grocery delivery startup (Tidewater Fresh)
prompt: I’m the head of growth at Tidewater Fresh and need a quick, data‑driven recommendation for our CFO, Elena Torres, on whether to raise our monthly subscription fee from $30 to $35 starting 1 November 2024. We currently have 9,500 active subscribers, each placing an average of 2 orders per month at $45 revenue per order. Also, a pending state regulation on single‑use delivery bags could add $0.15 per order, a cost we don’t yet know. Please give me one clear recommendation, outline the three biggest ways this plan could fail, and tell me what metric or outcome would make us stop or pivot.

setting: a payroll software company for small restaurants (Acme Payroll)
prompt: I need a quick, data‑driven opinion for Maya Patel, our CFO, on whether we should raise the base price of Acme Payroll for small restaurants from $12 per employee per month to $15 starting 2024‑05‑01. setting: a pediatric telehealth clinic network (Northwind Kids Health)

setting: a 40-person logistics software company selling to freight brokers (Brightline Freight)

setting: a regional bank's small-business lending team (Harbor Trust)

setting: a county public library digital-services group (Alder County Library)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal for Alder County Library’s digital‑services group and need a concise brief for our Library Director, Maya Patel, to bring to the board meeting on August 12 2024. We’ve been running a pilot e‑book subscription that started on January 3 2024 at $9.99 per month. Our internal model assumes 2,500 active members by the end of the pilot, with an 80% conversion from current print borrowers to digital, and that 70% of those will stay subscribed after six months. At a per‑download cost of $0.75 we estimate annual revenue of $299,700 (2,500 × $9.99 × 12). The contract with the vendor is up for renewal on July 15 2024, and we’re considering a 10% price increase to $10.99. The unknown is the licensing fee for the new premium titles we want to add; the vendor hasn’t disclosed it yet. I need you to give Maya one clear recommendation (keep, raise, or pause the price change), outline the three main ways this plan could fail, and specify the result (e.g., churn >10% or cost per download >$1) that would make us stop or rethink the move. Also note any arithmetic or assumption issues you spot.

setting: a B2B cybersecurity training vendor (Redoak Secure)
prompt: I need to brief our CFO, Maya Patel, about a proposed price increase for Redoak Secure’s flagship training platform. Currently we charge $12,000 per seat per year, with an average contract size of 30 seats, giving $360,000 ARR per client. We have 48 clients signed as of 15 Sep 2024, generating $17.28 M ARR. Our CAC is $9,500 per seat, and churn over the past 12 months has been 6% annually. I’m assuming churn will stay at 6% after the change. The plan is to raise the price to $14,000 per seat starting 1 Jan 2025, which I calculate will add $2,000 × 30 = $60,000 extra ARR per client, boosting total ARR to $20.28 M. The additional revenue should cover the $1.2 M we expect to spend on a new compliance module by Q3 2025 and extend our runway by six months. However, we don’t know how many contracts we’ll lose in Q1 2025, possibly 0–5. I need one recommendation for Maya, the main ways this could fail, and the specific result (e.g., losing more than three contracts) that would make us stop or reconsider the price hike.

setting: an indie game studio with one hit title (Moth Lantern Games)
prompt: Hi, I'm the co‑founder of Moth Lantern Games. We have a single hit title that currently brings in $120,000 of monthly revenue and $85,000 of monthly operating cost, giving a $35,000 profit before a $10,000 marketing spend we forgot to include. Our CAC is $70, LTV is $220, and we see a 15 % month‑over‑month growth in active users. We plan to raise the base price from $9.99 to $12.99 on 2024‑11‑15, assuming the price change will not affect churn. The new pricing would raise average revenue per user (ARPU) to $14.20, which we calculate as a 42 % increase, but we may have mis‑added the $12.99 plus $1.21 tax. The board wants a recommendation for the founder, Maya, on whether to proceed, the three biggest ways the move could fail, and the specific metric that would cause us to halt or pivot (e.g., if churn rises above 8 % in the first month). The unknown is the revenue‑share clause the platform will demand after we submit the update – we have no firm number yet. Also, we assume the new pricing won't trigger any consumer‑protection review, but we haven't checked the 2025‑02‑01 compliance deadline. Please give a concise answer with the numbers shown.

setting: a home-solar installer expanding to a second state (Sunrow Energy)
prompt:
Maya Patel, VP of Operations, Sunrow Energy  
To: Alex Rivera, CEO  

Alex, we’re gearing up to launch in Oregon after our success in Colorado, and I need a concise go‑no‑go recommendation for the board meeting on June 1 2025. Our current annual revenue is $3.2 million with an average residential install price of $12,000. We expect to close 250 installs in the first twelve months in Oregon, based on a 30 % conversion assumption from the 800 qualified leads we’ve already generated. Oregon offers a $1,500 state tax credit per install, but the licensing fee for the new jurisdiction is $45,000 plus $12,000 in attorney fees we’ve budgeted. I’ve calculated that we’ll break even after 200 installs, assuming a net profit of $5,000 per job after labor and material, but I haven’t factored in the $1,200 average cost of additional permitting inspections we learned from a competitor’s case study. The real unknown is the exact permitting timeline—our contractor says it could be 4–8 weeks, but we have no firm data. Please give me: one clear recommendation (proceed, pause, or redesign), the main ways this expansion could fail, and the specific result (e.g., permitting delays beyond 6 weeks or profit per install dropping below $4,000) that would make us stop or change course.
